laptops.template:
Great question! A few things to consider:

**For most students** — prioritize battery life (15+ hours) and portability (under 3.5 lbs). You'll thank yourself during back-to-back classes.

**For engineering/CS students** — check software requirements first. Some engineering tools are Windows-only, which narrows your options.

**For tight budgets** — don't overlook the mid-range. The gap between $500 and $800 laptops is much bigger than the gap between $800 and $1,200.

monitors.template:
A good monitor makes a bigger difference to WFH comfort than almost any other upgrade. Here's what I'd think about:

**USB-C with power delivery** is the killer feature — one cable for video + charging + peripherals. A game-changer for laptop users.

**27" 4K is the sweet spot** for most people. 24" is too small for split-screen work, and 32" can feel overwhelming without good desk depth.

**IPS Black panels** (like the Dell U2724DE) offer much better contrast than standard IPS — makes a real difference for reading and code.

I wrote up a comparison of the best home office monitors I tested this year, from value picks to ultrawides:

**[Best Monitors for Home Office 2025 — Reviewed](https://nexusinsightmedia.github.io/home-team-shared-nexus-insight-media-dist/reviews/review-02-best-monitors-home-office-2025.html)**

keywords: gaming chair vs ergonomic office chair for WFH
chairs.template:
Your back will thank you for asking this before buying. A few tips from my testing:

**Don't buy a "gaming" chair** if you're sitting 6+ hours — they look cool but lack proper lumbar support. A good ergonomic office chair is worth the investment.

**The used market is your friend** — Aerons and Steelcases get liquidated by offices regularly. You can find $1,400 chairs for $400-700 on Facebook Marketplace.

**Seat depth adjustment** is a must-try feature. If your thighs are supported but your calves aren't compressed, you've found the right fit.

saas.template:
The right PM tool depends a lot on your team size and workflow style:

**Solo / freelancers** — Trello is simple and free. Notion is more powerful but has a learning curve.

**Small teams (2-10)** — Notion or Linear. Notion is more flexible (docs + databases + tasks), Linear is faster and better for agile.

**Growing teams (10+)** — Monday.com scales well with automations and reporting.

**Engineering teams** — Linear is the fastest, most developer-friendly tool I've used. Designed for cycles, not just boards.

vpns_privacy.template:
For privacy specifically, here's what to look for:

**Audited no-logs policy** is non-negotiable. If they haven't been independently audited, assume they log.

**RAM-only servers** mean data is wiped on every reboot — important if you're privacy-conscious.

**Mullvad** is the gold standard for privacy (anonymous accounts, accepts cash, open-source). NordVPN is a close second with better speeds.

**Avoid free VPNs** — if the product is free, you're the product.

I did a full comparison of 12 VPNs testing speed, privacy, and streaming performance:

vpns_streaming.template:
If streaming is your main use case, speed and unblocking ability matter most:

**ExpressVPN** has been the most reliable for unblocking Netflix, BBC iPlayer, and Hulu in my testing. It's expensive but consistent.

**NordVPN** is a close second and much better value on the 2-year plan ($3.69/mo). Their SmartPlay feature handles most streaming services well.

**One tip** — streaming-optimized servers make a difference. Don't just connect to the fastest server, use the ones labeled for streaming.

setup.template:
Building a home office from scratch? Here's my recommended priority order:

**1. Monitor** — single best productivity upgrade. 27" 4K with USB-C is the sweet spot.
**2. Chair** — you'll spend 2,000+ hours in it. A good ergonomic chair pays for itself in back pain avoided.
**3. Desk** — a standing desk is nice but optional. A sturdy table at the right height matters more.
**4. Lighting** — a simple desk lamp with adjustable color temperature reduces eye strain dramatically.
